edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of military service, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, since labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the king, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. That good soldier, always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, completely send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signals in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the king, to see the soldier prepared; the king is present, who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts, he, joyful for victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial: be more diligent, so that he may give fame in exchange for death.

rejected: a life of luxury and ease

pass_b_english: You have signed up for military service, so you are held by a bridle. Begin now by casting off your former deeds: a life of luxury, since hard labor with arms is imminent. You must obey the King's command with every virtue, if you wish to reach the final times with joy. A good soldier always expects rewards to be enjoyed. Do not coddle yourself; banish idleness completely, so that you may report daily to your commander. Be watchful beforehand; review the signals at dawn. When you see war, take up the agony at hand. This is the King's glory: to see the soldier prepared. The King is present, ready to reign because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts; He, joyful in victory, watches and appoints His own attendant. As for you, do not spare yourself in the fight against Belial. Be more diligent, so that he may render fame in exchange for death.

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B fail to translate 'Suspicit' correctly in the context of the sentence 'Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus / Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse.' In Pass A, 'suspects' is a literal but contextually incorrect translation of the Latin; in Pass B, 'watches' is used. However, the primary failure is in Pass A's translation of 'optato propter spem dominicaturum' as 'who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope', which is a redundant and poor rendering of the Latin 'optato' (desired/longed-for) and 'spem' (hope). More critically, Pass A translates 'Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli' as 'You, moreover, do not spare yourself in respect to Belial', whereas the Latin 'in Belian' (likely a corruption of 'in Belial') combined with the instruction to be 'impiger' (diligent/industrious) in the context of 'fame for death' implies the struggle against him. Pass B's 'in the fight against Belial' is an interpretive addition not present in the Latin text 'in Belian'. Most importantly, Pass A's translation of 'Suspicit' as 'suspects' is a semantic error in this context (it means to look up at or observe), and Pass B's 'watches' is a better gloss but the discrepancy between the two regarding the sense of the sentence 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' (He looks up/observes, and dedicates his own attendant to be [something/present]) is not reconciled.
uncertainties: 'in Belian' is likely 'in Belial' (OCR/transcription error in source)
reasons: Pass A translates 'Suspicit' as 'suspects', which is a mistranslation of the sense in this context; Pass B translates it as 'watches'.
Pass A translates 'optato propter spem dominicaturum' as 'who will dominate because of the hoped-for hope', which is a redundant and inaccurate rendering of the Latin 'optato propter spem'.
